prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of GLP-1 physiology and the identification of its active form, which made incretin-based treatment of diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: All six opening ballots placed GLP-1 first, and I do not treat that agreement as proof of merit. The merit lies in the work itself. It runs from proglucagon processing and the insulinotropic action of GLP-1(7-36), through the physiology of secretion and receptor signalling, to drugs that now change outcomes in type 2 diabetes and obesity, with cardiovascular and renal benefit beyond glucose control. The evidence has been independently confirmed across several agents and large outcome trials, so it is neither premature nor contested on efficacy. As a neurologist I also note the growing interest in central satiety signalling, which adds breadth. Holst (physiology and secretion), Drucker (proglucagon-derived peptide biology and receptor action) and Mojsov (the active peptide form) cover the discovery side, which is the part a Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine is best placed to recognise.
statement.case_against: The credit history is the weakest point. Mojsov's priority for the active peptide is disputed, Habener is not on the credited list, and Knudsen's design of long-acting analogues is what actually produced the drugs. Any three-person cap therefore leaves out someone with a substantial claim, and a prize built on the discovery side alone could be read as overlooking the drug-development step that created the clinical impact. A prize with a single GLP-1 part also leaves no space for a second achievement, so a strong candidate such as the unfolded protein response would have to wait.

responses.point: Sandberg placed Knudsen in the trio with Drucker and Holst in place of Mojsov, because the long-acting analogues connect discovery to therapy and the priority around the active peptide is contested.
responses.response: I take the point that without Knudsen's work there is no semaglutide or liraglutide, and I do not dismiss it. I still prefer Mojsov in the third place. The prize is for a discovery, and the identification of the active GLP-1 form is the discovery step on which all later pharmacology depends, whereas analogue design is development carried out inside a company. Putting Knudsen in would also push out either Holst or Drucker, whose physiological contributions I regard as the core. I accept that the priority dispute may weaken Mojsov's case, and I would want the committee to examine it directly rather than avoid it by substituting a development contribution.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius ranked TNF blockade (Feldmann and Maini) second as a clean two-person configuration with long clinical use, and she added IL-6 as a related alternative.
responses.response: I agree that the attribution is cleaner than for most candidates, and the maturity is not in doubt. My reservation is conceptual. The case rests on translating a known cytokine into a drug target, and the credited names leave out the work on TNF itself and on the antibody engineering. If cytokine blockade is to be recognised I would expect the committee to decide whether TNF and IL-6 are a single achievement. I would not put TNF ahead of the unfolded protein response on scientific originality, but I accept that its patient impact is larger, and I could support it if the committee judges clinical benefit to be decisive.

responses.point: Perlmann placed the unfolded protein response (Mori and Walter) second, as a thoroughly confirmed mechanism with a fair, compact two-person credit, and he also listed Horwich and Hartl on chaperonin-assisted folding.
responses.response: I agree with the strength of B014. The credit is clean, the mechanism is conceptually elegant, and it is relevant to diabetes, neurodegeneration and cancer. My qualification is that, unlike GLP-1, it has no approved therapy, so the case rests on the basic science. That is acceptable for this prize, but it is why I put it as an alternative to B027 and not ahead of it. I am less convinced that a prize for chaperonin-assisted folding adds much beyond B014, since the link to human disease is indirect and the two would partly overlap in proteostasis.

responses.point: El-Manira ranked optogenetics second because of its transformative effect on circuit neuroscience, while accepting that the allocation among the six credited names is contested and a clinical criterion is only partly met.
responses.response: Optogenetics has had a large effect on my own field, and I do not dispute the importance. But I see a real problem with it. The channelrhodopsin discovery and the demonstration of neuronal control are distinct steps by different people, and three laureates cannot cover them without excluding Bamberg, Boyden or Miesenböck. It is also a method more than a physiological or medical discovery, with clinical translation still at an early stage. I would not oppose it in a second prize part, but I do not think the credit problem can be resolved at this stage, and in my view that makes it a weaker choice than B014 or B039.

responses.point: Linnarsson ranked CAR-T second, noting the durable remissions and approved products but also the unresolved credit for the original chimeric receptor concept, which is outside the credited names.
responses.response: I share his view of the clinical importance of CAR-T, and I list it as an alternative for that reason. The omission of Eshhar and other originators of the chimeric receptor concept remains unresolved, and it affects fairness, not only completeness. Rosenberg's contribution is adoptive cell transfer more broadly and is not the same achievement as CAR design. If the committee goes ahead with CAR-T, I would want the credit logic stated explicitly instead of simply accepting the three credited names.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov or Knudsen belongs in the third position, and how heavily the priority dispute over the active GLP-1 peptide and Habener's absence from the credited list should count.

Whether the committee prefers one broad GLP-1 prize or a two-part prize pairing a smaller GLP-1 configuration with a basic-science discovery such as the unfolded protein response, given the three-person limit.
How to weigh established clinical impact (CAR-T, TNF blockade) against conceptual originality (unfolded protein response, cGAS-STING) when therapeutic translation is limited.
I cannot independently verify the credit history from the supplied materials.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. My documented co-authorship with Thomas Perlmann concerns dopamine neurons, Nurr1 and autophagy, and does not involve any credited name. My postdoctoral period with Paul Greengard also does not involve any shortlisted candidate. Both are disclosed for transparency, and neither requires recusal.
